#3275. AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security

As autonomous AI agents work together, verifying their actions, enforcing security policies, and maintaining accountability becomes increasingly difficult

Vishal Sharma is a Reader in the School of Electronics, Electrical Engineering, and Computer Science at Queen's University Belfast, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.

In a de-authentication attack on an aerial vehicle using a human- and agent-in-the-loop approach, an AI agent can quickly scan the active channel and autonomously intercept traffic, thus reducing the time to react and regain control.

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance.

However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP?

Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution.

Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust.

An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system.

There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals?

Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform.

Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration.

The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents.

Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability.

The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist?

Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space.

Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models.

To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub, we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system.

We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted.

But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component?

#3273. Moonshot AI rented Nvidia’s top chips in China, Bloomberg reports

Documents show a $65M deal for servers with B300 chips, which are barred from China.

Chinese AI start-up Moonshot AI signed a deal in August to rent servers fitted with Nvidia’s most powerful AI chips. The US does not allow these chips to be sold to China without a licence. The deal was revealed in financing documents seen by Bloomberg.

Moonshot, however, disputes that the documents are accurate, and the company said it has no business relationship with the company that owns the servers, and did not take part in or approve the financing.

According to the documents, the deal covers 32 Super Micro servers equipped with Nvidia B300 chips. They are kept in Qingyang, a city in western China that is one of the country’s national computing hubs.

The rental is worth 432m yuan ($64.8m), or about $2m per server. Bloomberg estimates that is roughly 350% more than the going rate in the US. B300 servers already sell at a premium in China.

The servers belong to Lingmeixin, a Beijing company whose website describes it as a distributor of DJI drones. To buy them, it took a 200m yuan ($30m) loan from Beijing Zhongguancun Bank. It used both the servers and its contract with Moonshot as security.

Lingmeixin bought the servers from a company that mainly sells alcoholic drinks, including the Chinese spirit Maotai, and has recently moved into AI. The documents do not show how it got hold of them.

After Bloomberg asked for comment, the records no longer mentioned Moonshot, and the media outlet also could not confirm whether anyone had obtained a US export licence.

Both US companies distanced themselves from the deal. Nvidia said the firms involved are not its customers and do not receive its support. Super Micro, for its part, said it does not do business with them and follows all US export rules.

Moonshot makes the Kimi AI models, and its Kimi K3 model is seen as one of China’s strongest. The company is planning to list in Hong Kong early next year.

The White House has already accused Moonshot of using banned Nvidia chips to train Kimi K3. Meanwhile, Washington has been mapping how China rents the chips it cannot buy, and trying to stop smuggling. Research firm SemiAnalysis estimates that hundreds of thousands of them have already got through.

The report adds to pressure on Nvidia this week. Its chief executive, Jensen Huang, has admitted an affair with a former Megaspeed executive whom US officials suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed is at the centre of a US chip-smuggling probe. Nvidia’s board has opened an independent investigation.

Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

#3268. AWS commits $100M in AI and cloud credits to expand health services

The five-year AWS Health Impact Initiative backs projects for underserved communities, women’s and children’s health, and nutrition.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) is putting $100M worth of AI and cloud technology into health projects for underserved communities around the world. The AWS Health Impact Initiative will run for five years.

Rather than cash, organisations receive credits to use AWS’s AI tools, AI agents and cloud computing. Health charities, government bodies, researchers and companies can all apply, from early prototypes to full services.

The aim is to stop the gap in health care from growing as AI spreads. According to the World Economic Forum, generative AI use will grow faster in health care than in any other sector. If organisations serving poorer communities fall behind, AWS warns, health inequalities will widen.

“Agents and AI are revolutionizing health services, but these transformative technologies too often don’t reach the communities that need them most unless organizations know how to access and deploy them,” said Dr. Rowland Illing, chief medical officer and director, Healthcare and Life Sciences at AWS.

Too often, however, these tools do not reach the communities that need them most, Illing added. The initiative is meant to help the organisations that serve them build with AI.

Although the programme funds health projects of all kinds, it focuses on three areas. The first is wider access to care, from community health workers to hospitals, especially in rural areas and in low- and middle-income countries.

The second is research into women’s and children’s health. Only 5% of health research funding goes to women’s health, and up to half of the medicines given to children have not been clinically tested on them, AWS said. The third is access to healthy food, as a quarter of children worldwide have stunted growth because of poor nutrition.

Among current users, Eve’s Ark saves women’s health research data that might otherwise be lost when labs close or grants end, and has stored a petabyte of it so far.

In India, the Akshaya Patra Foundation uses AWS to run kitchens that serve school meals to more than 2.35 million children each school day.

Successful applicants get credits based on their estimated costs, or up to $10,000 to get started. The credits last 12 months and can be extended to 24.

The programme follows AWS’s Health Equity Initiative, launched in 2021, which gave $60m in credits to more than 400 organisations. Since then, AWS says it has supported more than 600 health groups in over 80 countries.

The launch also adds to Amazon’s wider push into health care. Its Health AI assistant recently opened to all US customers, and it has launched an AI Bio platform for early drug discovery.

AI is helping scientists rethink cancer treatment and the results are promising

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

AI is already integrated into our lives in many ways. It's changing the way we work, search and communicate. And while that kind of AI use may not be for everyone, perhaps one thing we can all agree on is how it is progressing medicine through breakthroughs that may have not happened without it. At least, not as quickly.

Researchers are using AI to understand cancer at a level of detail that would have been difficult to imagine just a decade ago. Rather than treating every patient with the same type of cancer in the same way, scientists are working toward treatments based on the unique genetic makeup of each person's tumor.

And there are encouraging signs that more personalized cancer treatments could make a real difference. In October, researchers reported promising Phase 3 clinical trial results for an experimental personalized cancer vaccine developed by Moderna and Merck.

When combined with the immunotherapy drug Keytruda, the vaccine reduced the relative risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% compared with Keytruda alone.

The vaccine isn't FDA-approved yet, and the trial doesn't establish that generative AI invented the treatment. But the results offer an important example of what personalized cancer medicine can achieve.

Meanwhile, AI is helping researchers tackle another part of the challenge: understanding exactly what makes one person's cancer different from another's.

One of the biggest challenges in treating cancer is that two people with the same diagnosis can respond very differently to the same medication.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

That's partly because cancer isn't a single disease. Even tumors that appear similar can have different genetic mutations, making one treatment effective for one patient and less useful for another.

A study within the last six months highlights that instead of relying solely on patterns found across thousands of patients, researchers can increasingly investigate the biological characteristics of a specific person's tumor.

AI is particularly useful because it can analyze enormous quantities of genetic information and identify relationships that might otherwise be missed.

The National Cancer Institute has already demonstrated one approach. Its PERCEPTION AI tool analyzes gene activity in individual cancer cells to predict whether certain drugs might work.

This is a significant breakthrough since tumors can contain different populations of cells. A drug might successfully attack some while leaving others behind, potentially allowing the cancer to return or develop resistance.

Tools like PERCEPTION could eventually help doctors understand those differences before deciding which treatment to recommend.

Another significant development involves AlphaFold, the AI system developed by Google DeepMind.

Proteins play a central role in how cells function, including how cancer develops and spreads. Understanding their three-dimensional structures can help scientists determine how potential drugs might interact with them.

Traditionally, identifying those structures could take years of laboratory work. AlphaFold can predict many protein structures in minutes, giving researchers a much faster starting point.

Google DeepMind has made predictions for more than 200 million protein structures available to researchers worldwide. And while that doesn't mean AlphaFold can automatically create a safe or effective cancer drug, scientists still need to determine whether predicted interactions work in laboratory experiments and, eventually, in patients. It can however, possibly help narrow narrow down the possibilities, potentially saving researchers significant time during the earliest stages of drug development.

For patients and families, the questions to ask are whether the advances in AI and personalized medicine will actually lead to better treatments. The recent melanoma vaccine results offer one encouraging example of the broader shift toward individualized care.

The experimental vaccine, called intismeran autogene, is designed using genetic mutations found in a patient's tumor. Those mutations help identify cancer-specific proteins that the immune system can learn to recognize.

In the Phase 3 trial involving 1,137 patients whose melanoma had been surgically removed, 82% of those receiving the personalized vaccine alongside Keytruda remained free of recurrence at two years, compared with 70% receiving Keytruda alone, according to Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center.

If AI can make analyzing that information faster, more accurate and more accessible, it could help expand the possibilities for personalized medicine.

There is still a considerable gap between discovering a promising treatment and making it available to patients. Even when AI identifies a potential drug or predicts how a tumor might respond, those findings need to be validated. Clinical trials remain essential for demonstrating that a treatment is both safe and effective.

There are also practical challenges, including the costs of genetic testing, access to specialized facilities and ensuring that AI systems perform reliably across different patient populations.

Yet, it's clear that AI is giving scientists new ways to study cancer, identify possible drug targets and predict which treatments may work best for particular patients. At the same time, personalized therapies are beginning to show meaningful results in large clinical trials.

The goal isn't to replace oncologists, but to give doctors better information and more treatment options.

#3264. Dresden AI chipmaker Sparxity closes Series A, taking funding to $90M

Sparxity, a Dresden company that builds computer chips and systems for AI, has closed its Series A funding round. The round brings the company’s total raised to $90M.

Yet Sparxity did not say how much of that came from the Series A.

ICM HPQC Fund, which invests in computing and quantum infrastructure, led the round. Lockheed Martin Ventures, chipmaker GlobalFoundries, GS Futures, Cloudberry Ventures, TGFS and the EIC Fund also took part.

Angel investors include Richard Socher, founder of Recursive Superintelligence, and Nancy Xu, whose start-up Moonhub was bought by Salesforce.

The company will use the money to develop chips for what it calls dynamic sparsity. Many AI models only use a small part of their network for each task.

Sparxity’s chips are designed to skip the parts that are not needed, which the company says saves time and energy. It is aiming for AI inference, the stage where a trained model answers requests, up to 44 times faster in very sparse models.

The company was founded in 2021 as SpiNNcloud, a spin-off from TU Dresden. It was built on SpiNNaker2, a chip inspired by how the brain works. Last month, it changed its name to Sparxity to reflect its new focus on sparse computing.

Sparxity said it has made more than 70,000 chips across three chip designs and installed 12 racks of its systems. It has more than 30 customers, including some of the world’s largest supercomputing centres, and its revenue quadrupled between 2024 and 2025.

Its current systems are used for scientific computing as well as AI. On selected tasks, the company says they run some calculations 10 times faster and uses 18 times less energy for certain machine learning work.

Hector Gonzalez, Sparxity’s co-founder and chief executive, said the money will help data centres move from power-hungry designs to setups with chips built for sparse AI.

“Sparxity has demonstrated the ability to manufacture its technology and deploy systems with major customers,” said Matthew Gould of ICM HPQC Fund.

The funding follows two recent deals. In October, Sparxity installed a system worth several million dollars at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Germany, home of JUPITER, Europe’s first exascale supercomputer.

Last week, it signed a letter of intent with T-Systems, the business arm of Deutsche Telekom, to bring its technology into T-Systems’ data centres.

“We are looking forward to having Sparxity on board in our AI factory soon,” said Ferri Abolhassan, chief executive of T-Systems.

Sparxity has also received EU support in the past. In 2025, it was picked for the European Innovation Council’s accelerator programme, which gave it €10m in grants and equity.

#3262. MagSafe Monday: Pelican’s MagSafe wallet is built for the people who still carry cash

I’ve been on a Pelican kick this fall. It started with the Pelican MagSafe Wallet, then the Pelican MagSafe Battery Pack, and the reason is pretty simple: once the weather turns cool, I want iPhone accessories built for the outdoors because I am outside more. The Pelican Protector Magnetic Money Clip Wallet is really helpful is you want something rugged, but also supports holding cash.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Most magnetic wallets are a simple card sleeve and nothing else. If you carry a few $5 bills for tips, cash-only places, etc., you end up folding them around a card and hoping they don’t slip out. The Pelican Protector Magnetic Money Clip Wallet has a stainless steel money clip on the outside of the wallet, so the cash rides on the back, where you can access it without pulling your credit cards out. It’s the same hard-shell construction as the rest of Pelican’s lineup, with the same MagSafe magnets.

The wallet holds up to five cards, which is just about perfect for my use cases. That covers my Driver’s license, debit card, and a few credit cards. There are ridges inside that push the cards up when you squeeze, so you’re not digging with your nails. A steel plate blocks RFID scanning, and the shell is rated IPX4 for water, which covers rain, etc.

Pelican calls its drop protection military-grade, which is what every accessory company says. A more useful way to think about it is that it’s a hard-shell wallet rather than a leather or silicone one.

Two things to know going in with this wallet. Five cards plus a clip of cash makes for a thick back on your phone, so this isn’t a very slim wallet. If you’re replacing a money clip, you are basically combining the two into one.

If you never carry much cash, the original Pelican wallet is the better pick. If you do want to carry a bunch of cash, the Pelican Protector Magnetic Money Clip Wallet is an awesome pickup.

The Pelican Protector Magnetic Money Clip Wallet is available on Amazon and directly from Pelican.

#3261. Adobe puts its Coworker AI agent in GenStudio, free for existing customers

Briefs, audience checks and on-brand asset versions now start with a chat. When Brand Intelligence and a human reviewer disagree, the human makes the call, Adobe told TNW.

Adobe’s AI agent for marketing teams, CX Enterprise Coworker, is now live inside GenStudio. That is Adobe’s software for producing and delivering marketing content. Teams ask it for what they need in plain language. The agent then carries the work across Adobe’s apps and the outside tools a team already uses.

Adobe announced the launch today at its MAX conference in Miami Beach. Coworker is free for existing licensed GenStudio customers, Adobe told TNW. All the new tools are available to customers worldwide.

It works across Adobe Experience Manager, Workfront, Brand Intelligence, Frame.io and GenStudio for Performance Marketing, depending on a customer’s licences. Teams can also use it as a standalone app, or inside Experience Manager, Workfront and Adobe Content Analytics.

Adobe says Coworker can draft campaign briefs, assess target audiences and produce versions of an asset for different channels and markets. It connects to other apps through the Model Context Protocol and Agent-to-Agent, two open standards for AI agents. Earlier this month, Adobe put the same agent inside ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot.

Varun Parmar runs GenStudio and Firefly Enterprise at Adobe. He said GenStudio has delivered more than 7.8 trillion assets so far this year. Adobe told TNW the figure counts every delivery of an image, video or 3D file to a website, app or other channel through Adobe Experience Manager. One asset can count many times. GenStudio manages more than 650 million assets for its customers.

Coworker draws on Adobe Brand Intelligence, an AI that learns a brand’s standards. It learns from written guidelines and from the unwritten knowledge built up inside a company. Teams can run brand checks straight from a Coworker conversation.

TNW asked Adobe what happens when the AI and a human reviewer disagree about whether a piece is on brand. Parmar said people make the call.

“Human judgment has the final say. Brand Intelligence gives people and agents the brand context they need and checks work against brand standards at a scale no team could manage by hand, but people set the guardrails and make the call,” Parmar told TNW.

He said the system learns from every review.

“The system learns from both written guidelines and the feedback teams give during reviews in tools like Photoshop and Workfront, so every decision a reviewer makes helps it better reflect how that brand actually thinks,” he said.

Brand Intelligence also gets a new feature called intelligent asset adaptation. It resizes and rearranges a design for other formats, such as a website banner or a mobile ad. The new versions stay on brand. Adobe is building Brand Intelligence into Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign and Firefly Creative Production for Enterprise.

Adobe backs the push with its own research, carried out by research firm Incisiv. It surveyed 607 marketing, creative and brand professionals at companies with $1 billion or more in annual revenue. It also polled 1,107 consumers and 304 business buyers in North America in July and August.

Staff closer to the work estimated that 27% of their company’s public-facing content is off-brand. Senior leaders put the figure at 9%. Adobe told TNW the gap shows how hard it is to keep to brand standards as the volume of content grows.

Of the professionals who approve content, 74% said they had signed off on off-brand work. Among those who had piloted automated brand-checking tools, 75% reported a mixed or negative experience.

In Workfront, Adobe’s project management software, a new Ideation Space gives teams a shared AI canvas. Coworker pulls past campaign results and product details onto it, and the team turns them into a structured brief. Adobe’s example is a retailer planning a Black Friday campaign.

Firefly Graph for enterprise lets teams build repeatable creative workflows from Adobe’s apps and outside AI models. Two new features are in beta. Capsules turn a finished workflow into a simple app that anyone can run, and Node Publishing lets teams build shareable custom workflow parts.

Firefly Graph outputs will also carry Content Credentials tied to the organisation, which record where an asset came from. Adobe’s 3D Digital Twin, which makes digital copies of products, can now place them in new 3D scenes. Teams and agents can also change labels and materials, generate video and set custom lighting.

Adobe has added AI to GenStudio before, and it sells its creative tools inside ChatGPT. Xfinity is bringing Coworker into how it runs campaigns.

“Bringing Adobe Coworker into how we run campaigns gives us one place to direct the work,” said Christopher Grove, vice president of GenAI and creative tech at Xfinity.

#3260. iOS 27.3: Three new iPhone features coming soon

iOS 27.3 is currently in beta and packed with new features, here are three that will hit your iPhone when the update launches next month.

Apple Health is getting some big changes in iOS 27.3 for all Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhones.

The new Health app adds Insights and Longevity tabs that provide personalized and intelligent recommendations related to your health. New features include educational videos featuring clinical experts, at-home movement evaluations using your iPhone’s camera, the ability to order and log labs, and a lot more.

Apple originally tested the new Health app in the iOS 27.2 beta, but it was removed before the public launch. The company said from the start, though, that the app would return and ship later this year, now confirmed with iOS 27.3.

Apple Music adds a new ‘Selfie Sing’ feature in iOS 27.3 that’s clearly designed to be used on social platforms like TikTok.

Selfie Sing lets you create karaoke videos of yourself using the iPhone’s camera and Apple Music’s built-in lyrics feature. As seen above, the feature puts lyrics onscreen below your camera feed so you can sing along to your favorite songs then share your video on social.

It won’t be for everyone, but Selfie Sing is a fun addition that represents one of Apple’s few attempts at a social-centric offering.

When iPhone Duo launched, it included a variety of exclusive features related to StandBy mode. But with iOS 27.3, Apple is bringing these StandBy improvements to all iPhones.

Additionally, iOS 27.3 lets you create multiple versions of each face for easily swiping between them. These features won’t be new for iPhone Duo users, but it’s great to see Apple bring them to more iPhone models.

Which iOS 27.3 features are you most excited about? Let us know in the comments.

#3258. Apple to open new Developer Center in Istanbul as part of broader Turkey investment

Apple today announced a long-term investment in Turkey, with seven new facilities focused on app development and manufacturing set to open in the country starting next year. Here are the details.

In a press release issued on its Turkish Newsroom (via MacRumors), Apple today announced a series of long-term investments in Turkey.

The announcement comes as former CEO and current executive chairman Tim Cook visits the country, as he’s been sharing on X.

Merhaba Istanbul! What a stunning view from the Grand Bazaar this morning alongside talented creator Cem Başak. Thrilled to visit this remarkable country! pic.twitter.com/c4daBBXe1l

The company’s investment in Turkey will be three-pronged, with the opening of five new Apple Developer Academies, one Apple Developer Center, and one Apple Manufacturing Academy.

Apple says it will open five new developer academies across Turkey over the next three years, with the first opening in Istanbul in 2027, alongside its new developer center. The Apple Manufacturing Academy, meanwhile, is set to open in Ankara in 2028.

Here’s Cook commenting on today’s announcement (translation ours):

“Apple has been serving our customers and communities in Turkey for 35 years. With this new commitment, we are proud to support the next generation of innovative entrepreneurs in the years ahead. […] Turkey’s developer community is developing apps used around the world. Meanwhile, small and medium-sized businesses stand out as organizations creating opportunities throughout the country. This investment provides developers and businesses with access to the training and resources they need to take their brightest ideas even further, as well as to Apple experts.”

Apple explained that its developer academies will offer “free, intensive nine-month programs focused on coding, design, marketing, project management, and artificial intelligence technologies,” while the developer center “will provide developers, entrepreneurs, and start-ups with a hands-on learning experience by providing access to the latest tools, technologies, and resources, as well as Apple experts and events.”

As for its manufacturing academy in Ankara, which will mark the company’s first Apple Manufacturing Academy outside the US, it will “provide free training and consultancy to small and medium-sized businesses, students and innovative entrepreneurs.”

Led by Apple experts, the curriculum will help participants adopt AI and intelligent manufacturing techniques through courses on machine learning technology, predictive maintenance, advanced automation, and robotics, as well as interactive workshops on lean operations and production efficiency.

This iPhone app provides contactless sleep tracking, and it holds its own against my gold-standard Oura Ring 5

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I've been tracking my sleep with the Oura Ring 5 for the past five months and love its comfortable fit and reliable data, whether I’m monitoring my 3 a.m. wake ups or how long I spend in deep sleep. However, the Oura Ring 5, now from $399 at Amazon, does come at a premium price. Keen to see if it was possible to replicate the accuracy of the Oura without the high cost, I started testing free sleep tracking apps — and discovered one that could hold its own against the best sleep tracker we’ve tested, the Oura Ring 5. The good news? It's completely free, with no hidden costs or trial sign-ups; all you need is a smart phone and a nightstand.

Here's how this free iPhone app compares to my $499 Oura Ring 5 (the gold costs more), plus how I'm using its tracking data to better understand my sleep. Looking for a wearable sleep tracker instead? I've rounded up the top sleep trackers you can buy in this year's Black Friday sleep sales, too.

There are plenty of free sleep tracking apps out there, so I decided to test three popular ones against my Oura Ring 5. The Oura Ring 5 is a luxury smart ring with highly-sophisticated sensor technology that can monitor your sleep cycles, sleep duration, and sleep latency (in other words, how long it takes you to fall asleep).

So, not only I was looking a free app that could provide those metrics, I was looking for a free app that could provide those metrics accurately.

After the Sleep Cycle and SleepScore apps failed to dazzle me, I didn't hold out much hope for the Sleepwave app, which you can get for free at the App store. Still, a 4.6 star rating out of 5 from over 3,700 user reviews convinced me to give the self-proclaimed "best free sleep tracker app" a go.

The Sleepwave app is completely contactless; you simply put your iPhone on your nightstand or mattress. Its sleep tracking relies mostly on movements (for example, from tossing and turning) and breathing, which are picked up by patented motion-sensing technology, as Sleepwave maintains that motion indicates wakefulness.

When I woke up after using the app for the first time, my expectations were low. However, comparing the Sleepwave's sleep data to my Oura Ring 5's, I was blown away by the accuracy of its metrics. From my overall sleep duration, my time spent awake during the night (including how long my 3 a.m. wake ups lasted), my sleep stages, and sleep latency.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The metrics are all presented in a bright infographic format, which is easy to read. On top of these sleep metrics, the Sleepwave app also includes a smart alarm which wakes you up during light sleep in the morning (when you're naturally more inclined to wake up), so it feels less jarring than being awoken during deep sleep.

Plus, thanks to the iPhone's microphone, you can listen to recordings of your bedroom's nocturnal noises, including snoring, vehicles, or pets — handy if you're a light sleeper like me who wants to see whether it's noise that is waking you up at 3 a.m.

As mentioned above, I tested the Sleepwave's accuracy by using the app while wearing my Oura Ring 5 and then comparing the data the next morning.

Here's a comparison between data from the Oura Ring and the Sleepwave app, recorded on the same night:

I consider a result 5 minutes under or over the Oura Ring metrics as an accurate match. As you can see from the above table, all metrics (apart from the REM sleep metric) fell within the 5-minute threshold — a remarkable result from a free sleep tracker app that's up against a $499 smart ring.

Of course, there things that the Oura Ring can do that the Sleepwave can't. For instance, the Sleepwave doesn't provide a readiness score (which tells you how much your sleep quality has prepared you for the day), heart rate variability (HRV), a sleep chronotype (your natural circadian rhythm), and health and fitness readings.

Still, if your main goal is to understand how long you fall asleep for or how much deep sleep you're racking up, then I highly reccomend giving the Sleepwave app a try (I mean, it's free, so what have you got to lose?).

The Oura Ring 4 may have been usurped by 2026's Oura Ring 5, but it still shares plenty of the same lab-accurate sleep tracking features with its successor. Right now, you'll find discounts on the metallic finishes (such as Silver and Black), which are down to $249. A Gold finish, meanwhile, will set you back $279.99...but it is down from $399.99. As with the Oura Ring 5, you'll need to pay a monthly subscription of $5.99.

The Garmin Index Sleep Monitor is a comfortable armband from the brand best known for GPS systems and sports watches. We were impressed with its accurate sleep data and lightweight sleep comfort, but it's not a great investment if you want fitness tracking, too. You'll find the Index Sleep Monitor for $169.99 at Amazon, though we have seen discounts during holiday sales like Cyber Monday.

If you're looking for both sleep and fitness tracking (like the Oura Ring) but want something more affordable, then the subscription-free Fitbit Air offers fuss-free, all-round tracking. It provides detailed sleep reports for under $100 and its app is intuitive to use, too. However, be aware that its strap can feel a little bulky to wear to bed at night.

#3256. iPhone Duo vs. Galaxy Z Fold 8 Camera Comparison: Frolicking With Apple’s and Samsung’s Foldables

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

I snapped some photos in a dreamy garden with these passport-size phones to see how their rear cameras stack up.

There are a handful of things Apple’s iPhone Duo and Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 have in common. They both feature a passport-size design, two rear cameras and roughly the same battery capacity. They’re also two of my favorite phones I’ve reviewed this year.

The compact, book-style configuration feels like the future of foldables, and Apple and Samsung have each nailed their offerings. Both phones are incredibly versatile, giving you the option to quickly swipe through apps on the palm-sized cover display or open up to a more sprawling 7.6-inch inner screen that’s great for watching videos and multitasking. That innovation comes at a cost, though, with the Duo starting at $1,999 for 256GB and the Z Fold 8 starting at $1,900 for the same storage level.

There are some drawbacks to having a more compact design, namely when it comes to the rear cameras. There’s no telephoto camera on either phone, which can make the high price tags a little harder to swallow. Plus, the wide and ultra-wide cameras aren’t quite as capable as what you’ll get on premium non-folding phones such as the iPhone 18 Pro and Galaxy S26 Ultra, which have more advanced optical zoom capabilities and larger main-camera sensors.

Still, the iPhone Duo’s and Z Fold 8’s cameras are nothing to scoff at. The Duo has a 48-megapixel wide and 48-megapixel ultrawide camera, as well as a 12-megapixel selfie camera on the cover screen and a FaceTime camera on the inner display (Apple hasn’t shared the resolution). Meanwhile, the Z Fold 8 has a 50-megapixel wide and 50-megapixel ultrawide camera, plus 10-megapixel selfie cameras on the cover and inner displays. That means you should still get photos that impress, whether you’re in the brightly lit outdoors or in a dark, moody setting.

To compare the cameras, I took the iPhone Duo and Galaxy Z Fold 8 to Filoli, a historic house and garden in the San Francisco Bay Area. These are some of my favorite shots, highlighting the strengths and unique characteristics of each phone’s cameras.

Both phones do a great job depicting the vibrancy of the lush background, but the iPhone Duo has the edge here. It better preserves the detail in the stone bench and flooring, and the greenery takes on a deeper, more satisfying hue.

These photos turned out very similarly, and both are equally dazzling. But the Z Fold 8 image is slightly sharper, as seen in the lines on the tree bark and the brighter, more pigmented greenery and flora. So I’m giving this one to the Z Fold 8.

These portrait images highlight some of the key differences in color and tone between the iPhone Duo and Galaxy Z Fold 8. I prefer the richer blacks and more vibrant colors captured by the iPhone Duo. It also does a better job of keeping the raven in focus, allowing the bird to stand out more distinctly against the background and creating a more striking overall image. By comparison, the Z Fold 8 produces a softer, gentler look, with a more subdued overall tone.

I like the brightness of the iPhone Duo image, and while the Z Fold 8 shot has slightly deeper shadows, the hydrangeas are also more vibrant. The blues and greens pop more on the Z Fold 8, as does the sky, which is a little washed out on the Duo. So this one goes to the Z Fold 8.

I keep flipping on this one, but ultimately, the richer colors and texture on the Duo image have won me over. The iPhone’s camera tends to cast a warmer glow, as you can see in the stone benches, while the Z Fold 8 takes on a more neutral tone. In the end, the differences are subtle and a matter of personal preference.

And finally, here’s me unwinding with a book. By default, the iPhone Duo applies a pleasing background blur, which I appreciate for the added dramatic effect. (This effect can be disabled when taking a photo, but I rarely choose to do so.) The Z Fold 8, by comparison, keeps the distant lawns and forested hills in sharper focus, preserving those details remarkably well. Ultimately, I prefer the Duo’s approach, which keeps the book in sharper focus and makes it stand out from the background. That said, I do appreciate the Z Fold 8’s ability to capture finer details throughout the scene, particularly the crisp individual blades of grass.

Because I’m a fan of both the iPhone Duo and the Galaxy Z Fold 8, it’s difficult to wholeheartedly recommend one camera over the other. Each has its strengths, and there are moments where one preserves detail and color better than the other.

In general, photos from the iPhone Duo tend to have warmer tones and richer, deeper colors, which can also lead to more pronounced shadows. Meanwhile, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 often produces brighter images, though this can sometimes come at the expense of finer details. But these results can vary depending on factors such as lighting and angles.

Ultimately, both foldable phones deliver impressive results, and the choice comes down to which image characteristics you value most. Thankfully, you really can’t go wrong with either.

#3254. Want an iPhone Duo for the holidays? Apple’s latest stock update isn’t reassuring

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The iPhone Duo likely won't make it into Santa's sleigh this year. Here's what Apple had to say about it.

Apple is unsure when it will have more of its foldable iPhone Duo in stock for customers to purchase ahead of Black Friday and the holiday shopping season.

During Apple’s earnings call on Monday, Nov. 2, Apple’s chief operating officer, Sabih Khan, told investors that the company couldn’t say when supply of its new iPhone Duo would catch up with current demand.

Also: iPhone Duo hands-on: Some magical touches

“iPhone Duo is constrained as of today … We’re working hard to get this revolutionary new product into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible. But at this time, it’s really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance,” Khan told investors.

The stock and shipping delays were among the broader concerns on an earnings call riddled with questions about rising memory chip costs driven by the AI industry, according to reports from TechCrunch.

Also: iPhone Duo shortage watch: Changing wait times, buying limits, launch-day odds

Last month, the iPhone Duo (Apple’s priciest smartphone to date) sold out shortly after its official launch on Oct. 23. Apple told the Financial Times that demand for the new Duo was “nothing short of extraordinary” after the smashing sell-outs, though veteran techies like Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman posited that Apple knew it would encounter supply chain issues, yet it was still the plan all along.

Those who didn’t initially jump to preorder the new device or wait in line at an Apple store are still facing shipping times that extend into 2027. Some outlets are even reporting that carriers like Verizon have offered gift cards as apologies for the extended delays.

Apple CEO John Ternus signaled the company’s effort to meet demand for the iPhone Duo, announcing that Apple will be “deepening” its partnership with Perryman, a titanium producer supplying pieces for the device.

Also: iPhone Duo screen cracks: Serious issue or overblown? What we know

“We’ve been thrilled with the early response from reviewers and customers, and we are working hard to get iPhone Duo into customers’ hands as quickly as we can,” Ternus said during his opening remarks on the earnings call.

While the iPhone Duo snafu is a rare event for Apple, which traditionally has a strong reputation for a smooth supply chain, rising demand for memory chips is raising hardware costs across the industry, and it’s something Apple can’t circumvent. On the call, Khan noted that Apple has had to increase prices on numerous products, though he said those decisions were made rather “reluctantly.”

Back in June, MacBooks and iPads saw price increases of up to 25% due to rising hardware and chip costs.

As Apple works to iron out its kinks, customers may be looking elsewhere. Reports from Korea indicate that Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 sales jumped 20% in the week after the iPhone Duo became available, and recent reports of cracked displays are another strike for Apple.

Also: Want an iPhone Duo before 2027? Try this

So, Santa may not be able to deliver the iPhone Duo this year, but Samsung’s foldables may make it onto Christmas lists across the globe instead.

Fans of the Roku aquarium will need to find a new way to just keep swimming.

Roku users are about to feel like fish out of water, as fans of the platform’s classic Aquatic Life screensaver are discovering that the animation will soon be unavailable.

The popular animated screensaver featuring realistic aquarium life will be replaced by the Roku City screensaver on Dec. 1. Roku City is the platform’s signature purple skyline, featuring rotating digital billboards packed with brand sponsorships and clever pop-culture Easter eggs. (Seattle’s short-spined raccoon, Jimothy, has made an appearance.)

That doesn’t mean all fish-filled options have been flushed. Several third-party Roku wallpaper apps offer a variety of aquarium options to choose from. But if you’re sticking to what Roku itself provides on its streaming boxes, the move away from the aquarium screensaver also means switching to an alternative that’s filled with advertising.

A Roku representative didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Viewers who miss these specific fish can still watch a YouTube version of Roku’s Aquatic Life screensaver for as long as the company chooses to keep this nearly 3-minute video on the internet.

The Aquatic Life screensaver loss is a drop in the ocean compared to other changes at the streamer this year. Roku was purchased by Fox for $22 billion in June, which puts the streaming platform under the same ownership as Fox’s Tubi and Fox One channels. That deal is expected to close in 2027.

So, I’ve taken a look at what’s currently trending on Netflix and picked out three shows that deserve your attention this week. Whether you’re after a twist-filled spy thriller about a secret agent, a warm-hearted comedy set in a small Arctic community, or a gripping prison drama, there’s something here for you. The second season of “Black Doves” is here, which means you have six new episodes to binge-watch this week. Originally planned as a limited series, the spy thriller proved popular enough to earn a second outing, with creator Joe Barton and production company Sister returning for another chapter. I’d also argue it deserves a place among this year’s Christmas viewing, thanks to its wintry London backdrop, complete with sparkling festive displays and freezing streets. The story itself is far from cozy, but that contrast makes it an interesting choice for the holiday season.

Helen Webb (Keira Knightley) leads a double life as an undercover spy for a secretive organization that sells stolen intelligence to the highest bidder. When her secret lover is murdered, Helen teams up with her longtime friend Sam (Ben Whishaw), a professional hitman, to investigate his death. Season 2 sees Helen continue passing government secrets to the Black Doves as her husband Wallace prepares to become prime minister. When her handler, Mrs. Reed (Sarah Lancashire), becomes caught up in a plot to undermine her position, Helen reunites with Sam.

“North of North” is also back for season 2, giving fans another chance to spend time with its quirky Arctic community. The comedy-drama made history as Netflix’s first Canadian original series produced directly in Nunavut, and its distinctive setting is a big part of what makes it stand out. Director Anya Adams, whose credits include “Yellowjackets” and “Abbott Elementary,” helps bring plenty of personality to the ensemble. With the show already making an appearance in Netflix’s top 10, there’s plenty of reason to give this one a try.

Newly divorced, she’s also open to dating again, all while raising Bun.

Stream "North of North" season 2 on Netflix

“Rectify” is a critically acclaimed Southern Gothic drama that deserves more attention from fans of character-driven TV. The series was the first fully owned original scripted drama developed for SundanceTV and ran for four seasons, with 30 episodes in total. Its slower pace and cinematic approach give the story room to explore its characters in a way that feels closer to independent filmmaking than traditional cable drama. The show also received a Peabody Award in 2014, securing it as one of the standout dramas of its era.

Daniel Holden (Aden Young) is released from death row after spending 19 years in prison for the alleged murder of his teenage girlfriend. However, adjusting to life outside prison proves difficult, particularly as he faces suspicion and hostility from a community still divided over his alleged crime. Meanwhile, his younger sister Amantha (Abigail Spencer) stands by him, while other family members struggle to accept his return.

Netflix is adding a new Discover feature, which recommends tailored streaming selections. Here's how it works.

AI tools are all over the internet, in the workplace, in your apps — and now there’s one coming on Netflix. The streaming giant just announced a new AI feature for the TV app called AI Discover, which will help users find titles that match their moods and interests. It’s initially being rolled out to a small group of users in the US whose language is set to English. To find out if you have access, check your Netflix navigation bar for the word “Discover” with a red gem icon next to it and a “New” label.

Also: Roku is taking away a fan-favorite screensaver

The AI Discover tab will be centered around themes. You’ll be able to pick from a range of themes depending on what you feel like watching, or how long you want to watch. You’ll also see selections that match what you’ve been watching lately and what’s popular.

You can refresh the list of suggestions or dive deeper with more complex search prompts. If you’d like to start over, you can pick the “Something different” option. To support AI Discover, Netflix is also adding a new button next to Play and My List that’ll let you tune your recommendations. You can press this button to keep a recommendation or to request that you don’t be recommended a title again.

Most streaming apps already rely quite heavily on machine learning and AI algorithms to offer user recommendations, even if they’re not marketed as AI features. Though most rely on traditional AI algorithms, like Prime Video’s “Recommended for you” tab, they personalize title recommendations based on your viewing history, likes and dislikes, and rental behavior.

Other platforms offer generative AI and features more similar to Netflix’s AI Discover. For example, YouTube features Gemini-powered searches that let you ask complex questions or use open-ended prompts to get results you want.

Some smart TV interfaces — including including Roku, Fire TV, Google TV, and, coming soon, Apple TV — have also adopted generative AI in their operating systems to let you use voice search with more naturally worded requests, and the system generates cross-platform results.

While I am itching to test this feature to see just how accurate it can be, Netflix hasn’t made it widely available yet. The company will gradually grant users access over the coming weeks, so stay tuned.

#3249. Report: Apple saved over $5 billion in taxes through Singapore and Ireland in 2026

A new Financial Times report reveals how Apple saved billions in taxes in 2026 by shifting profits through Singapore and Ireland. Here are the details.

A few days ago, Apple published its annual Form 10-K, as required by the SEC, containing detailed information about its financial performance and operations for its 2026 fiscal year.

Included in the form, as the FT noted, is information regarding how Apple reduced its tax bill by billions of dollars through its operations in Singapore and Ireland.

For years, Apple’s tax arrangements in Ireland were the subject of scrutiny, culminating in a 2024 ruling by the EU’s top court that required the company to pay €13 billion in back taxes. Apple completed the payment in 2025.

That came a few years after Apple announced plans to bring most of its $252 billion in overseas cash back to the US, following tax reforms introduced during Donald Trump’s first administration.

Since then, to discourage companies from shifting profits to countries with lower tax rates, more than 130 countries have agreed to introduce a minimum corporate tax rate of 15% for large multinational companies, as part of a 2021 initiative coordinated by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

Under the agreement, companies that pay less than 15% in a particular country may face additional taxes to make up the difference. The new rules also resulted in an additional $2.5 billion in taxes for Apple in Singapore in 2026, according to the company’s SEC filing.

Ireland adopted the new rules in 2024, followed by Singapore in 2025.

Back to the FT’s report, it notes that new US accounting rules now require publicly traded companies to disclose when their taxes on overseas profits differ significantly from the 21% US federal corporate tax rate.

These new requirements revealed that Apple saved $2.7 billion in taxes through Singapore in 2026, surpassing the $2.6 billion it saved through Ireland.

If Apple had been taxed on all of its global profits in 2026 at the US federal rate, it would have incurred a total bill of $33bn — demonstrating the scale of the $5bn tax reduction it received from booking profits in Ireland and Singapore. The company incurred corporation taxes totalling $27bn this year.

The FT also noted that Apple’s effective tax rate in Singapore fluctuated around 10% between 2023 and 2025, but is expected to approach 15% under the new rules. Singapore’s standard corporate tax rate is 17%.

#3248. Wendy’s Just Released a Video Game Where You Can Win Fast Food

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

I won a medium fries by defeating a sinister robot that looked suspiciously similar to a McDonald’s french fry container.

Wendy’s has turned its red-headed mascot into a wisecracking warrior who battles evil french fry robots in a free mobile game called WendyQuest. The company announced the retro-style role-playing game on Nov. 4. The announcement came with a promotion where you can win codes in the game, which are redeemable for menu items like fries and burgers at Wendy’s locations.

WendyQuest is available to download on iOS and Android. Desktop users can get it through the Steam platform. Anyone can play the game, but the promotion is restricted to people who are 18 and up living in the US.

You need to sign up for a Wendy’s account to redeem a code. While the food you can win is free, it requires you to buy something when you go.

“Wendy’s has been a part of gaming culture for years, including on Twitch, Fortnite and Feast of Legends, but WendyQuest is the brand’s first fully owned video game,” a spokesperson for Wendy’s said.

In 2019, Wendy’s partnered with the online multiplayer video game Fortnite, as well as the video-streaming platform Twitch, for various promotions featuring the company’s mascot. The company even released a rule book for a traditional tabletop roleplaying game the same year, called Feast of Legends, as a free download.

I downloaded WendyQuest, and my daughter and I played it for a while. The blocky graphics are reminiscent of the home-console video games of the late 1980s and early 1990s. It plays a lot like a simplified version of the DragonQuest, Final Fantasy and Breath of Fire games from the era, only stuffed with fast-food branding.

Rather than the regular turn-based battles that come standard in the early RPGs, this game adds a timing element, where you need to press a button at the right time like you do in old golfing video games.

It’s not a bad game. The light humor is suitable for younger players, and it’s fun to play. Like many RPGs, you battle monsters to gain levels, search around the maps for hidden areas, buy items and talk to people in towns to figure out what’s going on.

It took us over an hour to complete the first region, Fryshire, and get the Fry Stone, which unlocks a promo code for medium fries, free with a purchase. But again, you have to sign up for a Wendy’s account on their website or on the company’s mobile app.

Video games have a long history of offering real-world prizes to players as promotions. Swordquest, a series of video games released in the early 1980s for the Atari 2600, famously held a contest where players tried to win actual treasure made of gold and jewels.

In 2015, a promotion for the video game Just Cause 3 offered players the chance to win a private island. Developer Square Enix clarified that it couldn’t guarantee that the island would be livable and that the winner would have to pay all the taxes involved.

The reward codes from WendyQuest expire seven days after you get them, and Wendy’s says the codes are first come, first served.

#3247. loanDepot: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Servicing rights sales and discounted debt buybacks reshaped the balance sheet, but whether that offsets weak housing demand remains open.

Now that I’ve flipped my calendar to November, I’m counting down to Christmas and planning how I’ll decorate my home.

However, I don’t stick to the usual festive tree and decorative lights; I always rely on seasonal houseplants to bring vibrant life into the mix. Apart from my Christmas cactus, a poinsettia is a must-have — it’s basically Christmas in a pot.

Step into any garden center in mid-November, and you can’t miss a sea of crimson. Poinsettias have officially arrived and are the bright spark of color that signals the holiday season is near. But picking up a pot before Santa slides down the chimney comes with a risk. Choose the wrong plant now, and you could be left with a wilted stem by Christmas morning.

So how do you choose the perfect poinsettia so it still looks good when Santa arrives in December? Here, David Denyer, flower expert at Eflorist, shares how to choose a poinsettia in November so it creates a perfect display right through to the New Year.

Whether you’re picking a poinsettia for yourself or as a festive gift, Denyer advises checking the center of the colored leaves, known as bracts. “You’ll see small yellow-green buds, which are the true flowers. If these are still tight and unopened, your plant is fresh and will last much longer.”

Did you know?The colored sections on a poinsettia look like flowers, but they’re bracts, often called modified leaves. The red ‘petals’ have developed to attract pollinators to the tiny flowers in the center. Bougainvilleas and passion flowers are two other plants with bracts that are easy to mistake for petals.

When you go to buy a poinsettia, Denyer says there are two red flags to watch for. He advises against buying a poinsettia with drooping, yellowing or missing leaves. It’s not a healthy start.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

There’s another danger sign to watch for before buying this festive plant. Denyer adds, “Don’t choose plants that have been displayed outside shops or near automatic doors,” and he adds, “they’ll most likely be damaged by the cold draughts already.”

It appears that poinsettias prefer to be snug rather than chilly, so to keep your poinsettia protected, Denyer recommends, “Be sure to keep your poinsettias warm by wrapping them for the journey home; they really don’t like the cold.”

Once you’ve picked a healthy poinsettia, it needs to be treated just right to keep it looking its best, which is why it helps to know that this plant is used to sunny climates.

“Being native to Mexico, it makes sense that poinsettias love warmth and light, so placement is crucial,” says Denyer. “Select a bright room, ideally near a window where it can enjoy plenty of indirect light, but without its leaves touching the cold glass.”

They thrive in temperatures between 59-70°F (15–21°C), but they don’t like sudden changes, so he says, keep them away from draughty doorways, radiators, fireplaces and open windows, as they’ll struggle otherwise.

This attractive indoor watering can holds 35 oz of water and comes in sage green with a decorative wooden handle and a gooseneck spout. The durable stainless steel is leakproof, scratch resistant, and anti-corrosive.

According to Denyer a poinsettia will hold onto its color for at least six to eight weeks, so a plant brought in mid-November should see you through until the end of December. If you wait until December to buy your plant, it will keep going until the end of January.

There are four main stages can help you keep a poinsettia alive beyond the festive season. Here, Denyer explains what to do and when.

Late winterOnce the bracts begin to fade, gradually reduce watering and let the compost dry out a little more between drinks.

AprilCut the stems back to around 4 inches (10 cm) and keep the plant somewhere warm and bright.

MayWhen new growth appears, repot into fresh compost, then water regularly and feed every couple of weeks throughout summer.

FallFrom late September, give your plant around 14 hours of complete darkness each night for eight weeks. Covering it with a box or popping it in a cupboard overnight will do the trick. This short-day treatment triggers the colorful bracts to develop in time for Christmas.

A committee of independent directors, working with outside counsel, will oversee the investigation, the board said in a statement. The US has tried to control China’s access to these advanced chips for years. The company had previously characterized Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang as “not unusual or unexpected” given that the CEO “talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

Sales trends worsened this year, however. Kimberly-Clark's third-quarter adjusted sales dropped 1.3% compared to a year ago. The company's adjusted gross margin got squeezed, contracting 1.3 percentage points.

#3239. How Smart Glasses Detector Apps Work, and How Much You Can Trust Them

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Detector apps can identify Meta’s glasses and similar devices by their Bluetooth signals, as long as they’re switched on, nearby and broadcasting.

Bluetooth devices announce themselves to nearby phones with short broadcast signals, which is how your earbuds show up when you open your phone’s Bluetooth menu. Smart glasses do the same thing, and apps such as Zuckoff listen for signals that match known models, then send an alert when one turns up nearby.

It’s a clever workaround for glasses designed to blend in. How useful it is depends on what you want it to tell you: The app can detect that a pair is close by, but not whether it’s recording. Still, that’s more notice than most people get today, especially if they haven’t spotted the glasses’ built-in LED indicator

Here’s how those apps work, what they reliably catch and what they miss.

Zuckoff, whose name takes a direct jab at Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, has joined a small ecosystem of apps such as Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner and Nearby Glasses that offer similar functionality — letting you know when someone has smart glasses activated and how close the device is, although they can’t tell you specifically whether someone is actively recording or using AI to pull up information. The apps detect approximate device proximity by sweeping local Bluetooth frequencies to locate vendor IDs, system identifiers and hardware signatures associated with smart glasses.

As Zuckoff’s website notes: “Glasses advertise loudest while powering on, pairing or leaving the case. Once paired to their owner’s phone, they can go quiet, so silence is not proof that nobody is recording, and a detection is not proof that anyone is. Signal strength gives a rough distance and no direction at all.”

Zuckoff’s developer, Pawel Szydlowski, said he was already working on projects that used Bluetooth to detect nearby devices and discovered the tech could be applied to smart glasses. “It’s just the same technology wrapped in a different paper,” he said in a video chat with CNET.

Recent reports have shown that smart glasses are being used for everything from bullying in schools to viral videos with unwitting subjects who don’t know they’re being recorded.

Since it launched in early August, the Zuckoff app has gotten 2,000 sign-ups, and Szydlowski is beta-testing an Android version he hopes to make available on the Google Play Store. The app also has a premium version for $10 a year that can run continuous detection checks in the background when the app isn’t in use.

But a booming ecosystem of DIY modifications and third-party hardware hacks is also giving smart glasses wearers unprecedented stealth by allowing them to disable the activation lights, either by bypassing the capture LEDs or by patching software to suppress system notifications.

Tech journalist Joanna Stern hosted a video showing the process in which a local hacker removed the LED light from her Ray-Ban Meta glasses for $100, allowing the wearables to secretly record without notice.

Detecting active smart glasses in public or private spaces adds a new layer of security awareness, but it raises an obvious dilemma: What do you actually do with that information? Once a detector app alerts us that smart glasses are nearby, it seems our only choices are to either leave the space or ask the wearer to remove the glasses.

Uttara Ananthakrishnan, an associate professor of information systems at the University of Washington who studies the societal impacts of technology, says we’re still figuring out the social norms around wearables like smart glasses. It’s impossible to know whether the person filming will behave responsibly, and the question of consent gets even thornier if children might be captured on video or in photos.

“Until we develop clear mechanisms to balance seamless innovation with consent, these devices will continue to turn everyday public spaces into zones of surveillance anxiety,” she said.

The Even G2 smart glasses don’t have a camera for recording photos or videos. They can pair with a separately sold R1 control ring that works as a fitness tracker.

For instance, Even Realities’ G2 smart glasses don’t include a front-facing camera at all. Instead, the Even G2 devices, released in late 2025, focus on providing the wearer with information and acting more like a personal assistant.

“We made the decision from the beginning that smart glasses don’t need to have cameras on them in order to be useful,” Even Realities CEO Will Wang told CNET in an email. “We believe something worn on your face should respect not only the person wearing it, but everyone around them.”

The G2 devices don’t record externally, a design choice Wang said gave the company a unique challenge. “Leaving the camera out also pushed us to think differently about what actually makes smart glasses useful day to day, rather than assuming more sensors automatically make a better product,” he said.

Wang said there’s room in the smart glasses market for different approaches to features and functionality, and that buyers may want to make trade-offs for devices they’ll wear on their faces. But Wang noted that the rise of smart glasses detectors indicates that social acceptance is an issue the industry needs to consider.

Over the last several months, smart glasses have been getting cheaper. And with more models and companies jumping into the fray, the demand for surveillance detectors is likely to grow — that is, unless Big Tech and wearable companies radically change their devices to make them invisible to detector apps.

Szydlowski said his hope is that, in time, Zuckoff won’t be needed at all. He pointed out that the ability to detect nearby Apple AirTag devices eventually became part of the operating systems on iOS and Android devices. If consumers pressure manufacturers and their governments to make smart glasses easier to detect, it would be “the perfect solution” to make his app obsolete, he said.
